items.stem: Classify each prenatal test as a Screening test or a Diagnostic test.
items.rationale_correct: Screening tests estimate risk (cfDNA, quad, GCT); diagnostic tests provide a karyotype (CVS, amniocentesis). Principle: a positive screen estimates probability and is confirmed by a diagnostic test.

rationale_distractors.(any swap): Labeling cfDNA 'diagnostic' or amniocentesis 'screening' confuses risk estimation with confirmation and misguides counseling.

items.stem: A patient's cell-free DNA screen returns 'high risk' for trisomy 21. How should the nurse explain the result?
options: It confirms the fetus has Down syndrome
It is a screening result that estimates increased risk and needs diagnostic confirmation
It rules out all other chromosomal conditions
key: It is a screening result that estimates increased risk and needs diagnostic confirmation
items.rationale_correct: cfDNA is a screen; a high-risk result raises probability but requires diagnostic testing (CVS or amniocentesis) to confirm. Principle: never treat a screening result as a diagnosis.

rationale_distractors.It rules out all other chromosomal condi: cfDNA targets specific trisomies, not all conditions.
rationale_distractors.It requires immediate pregnancy terminat: Directive and premature; counseling and confirmation come first.

items.stem: At which gestational-age window is a vaginal-rectal culture for group B streptococcus collected?
items.rationale_correct: GBS screening is done at 36 0/7 to 37 6/7 weeks so results guide intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. Principle: time GBS screening near term so the culture reflects labor-time colonization.

rationale_distractors.8 to 12 weeks: Too early to predict intrapartum status.
rationale_distractors.Only during active labor: Culture results are not available quickly enough in labor.

items.stem: A patient is offered amniocentesis for diagnostic testing. Which nursing action best supports ethical, patient-centered care?
options: Tell her she must have the test
Provide information and support her right to accept or decline
Perform the test without discussing risks
Decide for her based on her age
key: Provide information and support her right to accept or decline
items.rationale_correct: Diagnostic testing is elective; the nurse provides balanced information and supports informed, autonomous choice. Principle: informed consent means the patient may decline without coercion.

items.stem: An Rh-negative patient at 28 weeks with a negative antibody screen is being evaluated. Select the 2 nursing actions, the 1 condition being prevented, and the 2 parameters to verify before administration.

actions_options: Administer Rh(D) immune globulin as ordered
Educate about the purpose and timing of the injection
Withhold the injection because she has no symptoms

actions: Administer Rh(D) immune globulin as ordered
Educate about the purpose and timing of the injection

items.rationale_correct: Routine 28-week Rh(D) immune globulin prevents alloimmunization in an unsensitized Rh-negative patient; verify Rh-negative status and a negative antibody screen first. Principle: give anti-D before sensitization can occur, not after.

rationale_distractors.Give the rubella vaccine instead: A live vaccine deferred to postpartum, unrelated to Rh.
rationale_distractors.Blood glucose / Deep tendon reflexes: Relevant to GDM and magnesium therapy, not anti-D.

items.stem: An Rh-negative patient gives birth to an Rh-positive infant. Within what time frame should Rh(D) immune globulin be given postpartum?
options: It is not needed if she received it at 28 weeks
items.rationale_correct: Postpartum anti-D is given within 72 hours when the infant is Rh-positive, in addition to the 28-week dose. Principle: the postpartum dose covers the delivery-related fetomaternal bleed and is time-critical.

rationale_distractors.Within 2 weeks of birth: Too late; the 72-hour window is standard.
rationale_distractors.It is not needed if she received it at 2: The antenatal dose does not replace the postpartum dose.

items.stem: Reviewing a patient's prenatal record across visits, select the interpretation that should prompt further evaluation.

chart_data.visits: week 24: BP 116/72, weight +6 lb; week 28: BP 128/82, weight +9 lb; week 32: BP 140/90, weight +12 lb

options: Blood pressure and weight are trending normally
A rising blood pressure trend warrants closer evaluation
key: A rising blood pressure trend warrants closer evaluation
items.rationale_correct: A steady upward blood pressure trend across visits can signal an emerging hypertensive disorder and warrants evaluation. Principle: trend the prenatal record, not single readings, to catch developing problems early.

rationale_distractors.normal trends / decreasing fundal height: Each describes a different pattern; the recorded rising blood pressure contradicts them.

items.stem: A patient's 1-hour 50 g glucose challenge test is elevated. Which is the appropriate next step?
options: Diagnose gestational diabetes and start insulin
Proceed to the 3-hour oral glucose tolerance test
key: Proceed to the 3-hour oral glucose tolerance test
items.rationale_correct: An abnormal 1-hour screen is confirmed with the diagnostic 3-hour OGTT. Principle: a positive screen leads to a diagnostic test, not directly to treatment.

items.stem: In an uncomplicated pregnancy, which prenatal visit schedule should the nurse teach as typical?
options: Every 4 weeks until 28 weeks, every 2 weeks until 36 weeks, then weekly
key: Every 4 weeks until 28 weeks, every 2 weeks until 36 weeks, then weekly
items.rationale_correct: The traditional schedule increases visit frequency as term approaches to catch late-emerging problems. Principle: surveillance intensifies as risk of late complications rises.

items.stem: A patient asks the difference between chorionic villus sampling and amniocentesis. Which statement is accurate?
options: CVS can be done earlier (about 10 to 13 weeks) than amniocentesis (15 weeks or later), and both are diagnostic
key: CVS can be done earlier (about 10 to 13 weeks) than amniocentesis (15 weeks or later), and both are diagnostic
items.rationale_correct: CVS provides an earlier diagnostic karyotype than amniocentesis; both are diagnostic, not screening. Principle: choose the diagnostic test by gestational-age timing and clinical need.

items.stem: The quad screen is typically performed during which gestational-age window?
items.rationale_correct: The quad screen is drawn at 15 to 22 weeks. Principle: match each screening test to its correct timing window.

rationale_distractors.6 to 10 weeks: Too early for the quad screen.

items.stem: A patient's quad screen returns 'screen positive.' Which nursing explanation is most accurate?
options: The fetus definitely has a chromosomal abnormality
The result indicates increased risk and diagnostic testing can be offered
key: The result indicates increased risk and diagnostic testing can be offered
items.rationale_correct: A positive quad screen raises risk and prompts an offer of diagnostic testing; it does not diagnose. Principle: a positive screen is a probability statement, not a verdict.

items.stem: Rh(D) immune globulin is routinely offered to an unsensitized Rh-negative patient at which point in pregnancy?
items.rationale_correct: Routine antenatal anti-D is given around 28 weeks, with an additional postpartum dose if the infant is Rh-positive. Principle: the 28-week dose prevents third-trimester sensitization.

rationale_distractors.At 12 weeks: Earlier than the routine antenatal dose.

items.stem: Select all situations in which an Rh-negative, unsensitized patient should receive Rh(D) immune globulin.
options: Within 72 hours of birth if the infant is Rh-positive
key: Within 72 hours of birth if the infant is Rh-positive
items.rationale_correct: Anti-D is indicated at 28 weeks and after any sensitizing event — loss, invasive procedure, or Rh-positive birth. Principle: any fetomaternal bleeding in an Rh-negative patient triggers anti-D.

rationale_distractors.When the patient is Rh-positive: Rh-positive patients cannot be sensitized to D and do not need anti-D.
